questions.stem: Under the double entry system of book-keeping:

options.text: Every transaction is recorded with a debit in one account and an equal credit in another
options.explanation: Correct. Every transaction has a two-sided character — benefit received and benefit given — so one account is debited and another credited with an equal amount, always.

options.text: Every transaction is recorded in two different books
options.explanation: Two ACCOUNTS, not two books — both aspects can even sit in the same book (a contra entry lives entirely inside the cash book).

options.text: Only cash transactions are recorded in full; credit transactions wait for settlement
options.explanation: That is single-entry (incomplete records) thinking. Double entry records credit transactions immediately and completely.

options.text: Every transaction is recorded twice in the same account, once on each side
options.explanation: That would cancel the entry to nothing. The two aspects go to two DIFFERENT accounts, one on each side.

questions.sourceRef: Double entry: every debit has an equal and corresponding credit

questions.stem: Under the traditional classification, Outstanding Salaries A/c is best classified as a:

options.explanation: Real accounts cover properties and possessions (cash, machinery, goodwill) — an amount owed to employees is not a possession.
Correct. It LOOKS like an expense but actually stands for the employees to whom salary is owed — a group of persons — so it is personal (representative), not nominal.
Artificial personal accounts are bodies like firms, banks and clubs. Outstanding salaries REPRESENTS natural persons collectively — that makes it representative, not artificial.
The salary EXPENSE is nominal; the OUTSTANDING amount represents the persons still to be paid — the classic representative-personal trap.

questions.sourceRef: Representative personal accounts: outstanding/prepaid items stand for persons

questions.stem: Capital A/c and Drawings A/c are:

options.explanation: Neither is an expense or income of the business — both belong to the owner, a person. This is one of the most-missed classifications in the section.
Real accounts are properties and possessions. Capital is what the business OWES the owner — a personal account relationship.
Correct. Both accounts belong to the owner — a person — so both are personal accounts, even though drawings feels like an 'expense' and capital feels like a 'fund'.
Drawings is money the OWNER takes out — it reduces what the business owes the owner. It is personal, not a business expense.

questions.sourceRef: Capital and Drawings = personal accounts of the owner

questions.stem: Meena General Stores keeps an account with Nashik Urban Co-operative Bank. In Meena's books, the Bank A/c is a:

options.explanation: Representative personal accounts stand for a GROUP of persons behind an item (outstanding salaries). The bank is itself one artificial person, dealt with directly.

options.text: Real account, because bank balance is money
options.explanation: It FEELS like money, but the account records a relationship with the bank — an artificial person that owes Meena her balance. That makes it personal.
Nominal accounts are expenses, losses, incomes and gains — a bank balance is none of these.
Correct. The bank is an artificial person (like a firm or a club); the account tracks what it owes Meena (or what she owes it, on overdraft).

questions.sourceRef: Bank = artificial personal account, not real

questions.stem: The golden rule for NOMINAL accounts is:

options.text: Debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains
options.explanation: Correct. Nominal accounts are the expense/loss and income/gain accounts, and this rule sets their directions.

options.text: Debit what comes in, credit what goes out
options.explanation: That is the rule for REAL accounts — it needs a property or possession to move.

options.text: Debit the receiver, credit the giver
options.explanation: That is the rule for PERSONAL accounts — it needs a person to receive or give.

options.text: Debit all incomes and gains, credit all expenses and losses
options.explanation: Reversed — this would show rent paid as a credit. Expenses and losses are DEBITED.

questions.sourceRef: Golden rules — nominal: debit expenses/losses, credit incomes/gains

questions.stem: Under the modern (accounting equation) classification, an INCREASE in a liability is recorded as a ______ and a DECREASE in an asset as a ______:

options.explanation: The asset half is right, but liabilities INCREASE on the credit side — debiting a liability reduces it.
Correct. Liabilities rise by credit; assets rise by debit, so a FALL in an asset is a credit. (Example: buying goods on credit — creditor up (credit), and when later paid, cash down (credit).)
The liability half is right, but a decrease in an asset is a CREDIT — debit is the direction in which assets grow.
Both reversed — this applies the asset rule to liabilities and the liability rule to assets.

questions.sourceRef: Modern map: liability increase = credit; asset decrease = credit

questions.stem: On 1 April 2026 the books of Sethi Kirana Stores, Indore show: cash ₹12,000, bank ₹58,000, stock ₹90,000, debtors ₹45,000, furniture ₹35,000, creditors ₹60,000 and a bank loan of ₹30,000. In the opening entry, Capital A/c is credited with:

options.explanation: This credits the whole of the assets to Capital and forgets that the creditors and the loan take their own credits of ₹90,000 in the same compound entry.
This also deducts the furniture of ₹35,000, treating a fixed asset as if it were a liability. Furniture is debited in the opening entry like every other asset.

Correct. Total assets = 12,000 + 58,000 + 90,000 + 45,000 + 35,000 = 2,40,000; total liabilities = 60,000 + 30,000 = 90,000; opening capital = 2,40,000 − 90,000 = ₹1,50,000 — the balancing figure of the opening entry.
This ADDS the liabilities to the assets instead of deducting them — capital is assets MINUS liabilities.

questions.sourceRef: Opening capital = total assets − total liabilities

questions.stem: Meena buys a weighing machine from Zenith Engineering for ₹84,000, paying ₹50,000 by cheque and leaving the balance on credit. In the compound journal entry, Zenith Engineering's account is credited with:

options.explanation: This credits Zenith with the full price — but Bank already takes a credit of ₹50,000 in the same entry, so total credits (1,34,000) would exceed the debit of 84,000.
This swaps the two credits — ₹50,000 is what went out of the BANK; Zenith is owed only the unpaid balance.
This splits the price into equal halves instead of using the actual cheque figure given — the balance owed is 84,000 − 50,000, not 84,000 ÷ 2.
Correct. Machinery A/c Dr 84,000 — To Bank A/c 50,000, To Zenith Engineering A/c 34,000 (84,000 − 50,000). Total debits still equal total credits.

questions.sourceRef: Compound entry: one debit, several credits; balance to supplier

questions.stem: Divya Traders, Pune journalises for April 2026: business started with cash ₹2,50,000; goods bought for cash ₹30,000; goods sold on credit to Farhan ₹42,000; rent paid in cash ₹8,000. The total of the DEBIT column of these journal entries is:

options.explanation: Correct. Debits: Cash 2,50,000 + Purchases 30,000 + Farhan 42,000 + Rent 8,000 = ₹3,30,000 — and the credit column must total the same before you move on.
This omits the credit sale to Farhan (2,50,000 + 30,000 + 8,000) — treating a transaction with no cash movement as unrecordable. Double entry records credit transactions immediately.
This adds the debit AND credit columns together — each column separately totals 3,30,000; the question asks for one column.
This omits the rent payment of ₹8,000 — an expense is debited like any other aspect (3,30,000 − 8,000).

questions.sourceRef: In any batch of entries, total debits = total credits

questions.stem: Which statement about the journal is CORRECT?

options.text: The L.F. column records the invoice number of the transaction
options.explanation: L.F. (ledger folio) records the PAGE of the ledger where each account lives — the cross-reference between journal and ledger.

options.text: It is the book of original entry, recording transactions chronologically with a narration for each
options.explanation: Correct. Transactions enter the journal (or the relevant subsidiary book) FIRST, in date order, and are then posted to the ledger.

options.text: It is the principal book, showing each account's complete story in one place
options.explanation: That describes the LEDGER. The journal records both aspects of each transaction together; the ledger separates them account by account.

options.text: Transactions are first recorded in the ledger and then journalised
options.explanation: Reversed — the flow is journal → ledger (posting), never the other way.

questions.sourceRef: Journal = chronological book of original entry; L.F. = ledger page

questions.stem: Divya Traders sold goods on credit to Farhan for ₹42,000. Farhan later returned goods worth ₹4,000 and paid ₹25,000 in cash. On balancing, Farhan's account shows:

options.explanation: This deducts the returns twice (42,000 − 4,000 − 4,000 − 25,000) — each aspect is posted once.
Side flipped. The c/d entry does sit on the credit side, but the balance is NAMED by the b/d side — here the debit side was heavier, so it is a debit balance.
Correct. 42,000 − 4,000 − 25,000 = ₹13,000; the debit side is heavier, so Farhan is a debtor for ₹13,000. Balance c/d sits on the credit (lighter) side; b/d reopens on the debit side.
This forgets the sales returns of ₹4,000 (42,000 − 25,000) — returned goods reduce what Farhan owes.

questions.sourceRef: Balancing: difference on lighter side as c/d; b/d side names the balance

questions.stem: A ledger account has: debit side — opening balance ₹10,000 and sales ₹35,000; credit side — cash received ₹28,000 and returns ₹2,000. After writing the Balance c/d and ruling off, EACH side of the account totals:

options.explanation: This adds both sides together (45,000 + 30,000) — each side is totalled separately, and both are made to agree at 45,000.
That is the Balance c/d itself (45,000 − 30,000), not the ruled-off total of each side.
This totals only the credit entries (28,000 + 2,000) — after the c/d is inserted, both sides are made equal to the HEAVIER side's total.
Correct. The heavier (debit) side totals 10,000 + 35,000 = 45,000; the c/d of 15,000 is written on the lighter (credit) side so that BOTH sides total ₹45,000.

questions.sourceRef: Ruled-off totals = heavier side's total, both sides

questions.stem: In ledger accounts, the prefixes 'To' and 'By':

options.text: Are pure convention — 'To' before entries on the debit side, 'By' on the credit side
options.explanation: Correct. The prefixes carry no meaning beyond marking the side; each entry names the OTHER account of the double entry.

options.text: Identify the receiver and the giver under the personal-account rule
options.explanation: The golden rules decide WHICH account is debited; 'To'/'By' merely decorate the entries once the side is chosen.

options.text: Mean money paid TO someone and received BY someone
options.explanation: Tempting, but no — 'To Sales A/c' in a debtor's account involves nobody being paid. The words are tradition only.

options.text: Are compulsory under the Companies Act
options.explanation: No law prescribes them — this chapter quotes no statute; the prefixes are bookkeeping custom.

questions.sourceRef: 'To' = debit side, 'By' = credit side — convention only

questions.stem: At year end, which accounts are NOT balanced and carried forward to the next year?

options.explanation: The bank account is a personal account and its balance certainly carries forward — you do not lose your bank balance at midnight on 31 March.
Correct. Expenses and incomes are closed by transfer to the Trading and Profit & Loss Account — a fresh year starts them at nil. Only personal and real accounts carry balances forward.
Debtors, creditors, capital — all personal accounts carry forward; the relationships continue into the new year.
Real accounts (cash, machinery, stock) carry their balances forward — they feed the next year's opening entry.

questions.sourceRef: Nominal accounts close to Trading/P&L; personal and real carry forward

questions.stem: Sethi Stores, a cloth merchant, had these March transactions: (i) cloth bought on credit from Anand Mills, list price ₹40,000 less 10% trade discount; (ii) cloth bought for cash ₹12,000; (iii) a computer bought on credit from Digitek ₹25,000; (iv) cloth bought on credit from Bharat Textiles ₹18,000. The total of the PURCHASES BOOK is:

options.explanation: This includes the cash purchase of ₹12,000 — cash purchases belong to the cash book, never the purchases book.
This includes the computer (54,000 + 25,000) — a credit purchase of an ASSET goes to the journal proper, because computers are not what a cloth merchant trades in.

Correct. Only credit purchases of GOODS qualify: Anand Mills net of trade discount (40,000 − 4,000 = 36,000) + Bharat Textiles 18,000 = ₹54,000. The cash purchase goes to the cash book; the computer goes to the journal proper.
This records Anand Mills at the gross list price of 40,000 — trade discount is deducted on the invoice and the entry is made NET; it never appears in any account.

questions.sourceRef: Purchases book: credit purchases of goods only, net of trade discount

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Accounting Process · Trade vs cash discount
questions.stem: Rhea Fabrics sells goods to Kanchan on credit: list price ₹50,000 less 15% trade discount, with a further 2% cash discount offered for payment within 10 days. The amount entered in the SALES BOOK is:

options.explanation: This records the gross list price — trade discount is deducted on the invoice itself and never appears in any account.
That is the trade discount itself — the one figure guaranteed never to appear in any account or book.
This deducts the cash discount too (42,500 × 0.98) — but at the point of sale no payment has happened; cash discount belongs to the settlement, not the sale.

Correct. Entries are made NET of trade discount: 50,000 − 7,500 = ₹42,500. The cash discount is recorded only if and when Kanchan actually pays within the period — nothing about it enters the sales book.

questions.sourceRef: Trade discount: recorded net; cash discount: recorded at settlement

questions.stem: Office furniture bought on credit from Modern Furnishers by a cloth merchant should be recorded in:

options.explanation: Correct. Credit purchases and sales of ASSETS are among the leftovers the journal proper keeps — furniture is not what a cloth merchant trades in.
The purchases book takes only credit purchases of GOODS traded in. Left here, Furniture ends up debited to Purchases A/c — an error of principle that overstates expenses and understates assets.
No cash or bank moved — the purchase is on credit. The cash book records only cash and bank movements.
Nothing was sold — and the sales book takes only credit sales of goods anyway.

questions.sourceRef: Credit purchase of an asset → journal proper

questions.stem: The source document for recording entries in the SALES RETURNS (returns inward) book is the:

options.explanation: Pay-in slips evidence bank deposits and support the cash book.
Correct. When a customer sends goods back, the seller issues a credit note (the customer's account will be credited) — that document feeds the sales returns book.
The outward invoice supports the SALES book — the original sale, not the return.
A debit note supports the PURCHASE RETURNS book — the buyer 'debits' the supplier when sending goods back.

questions.sourceRef: Sales returns book ← credit note; purchase returns book ← debit note

questions.stem: The purchases book records:

options.text: All purchases made by the firm, whether of goods or assets
options.explanation: Two filters apply, and this fails both: only GOODS (things traded in), and only on CREDIT.

options.text: Credit purchases of goods and of assets
options.explanation: A machine bought on credit is not 'purchases' — assets on credit go to the journal proper.

options.text: Only credit purchases of goods dealt in by the firm
options.explanation: Correct. Both filters are strict: credit transactions only, and goods (the firm's trading stock) only. Cash purchases → cash book; credit asset purchases → journal proper.

options.text: Cash and credit purchases of goods
options.explanation: Cash purchases go to the cash book — the purchases book never sees them.

questions.sourceRef: Goods books take only credit transactions of goods

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Accounting Process · Trade vs cash discount
questions.stem: Which statement about TRADE discount is correct?

options.text: It appears in the discount columns of the triple-column cash book
options.explanation: The discount columns hold CASH discount (allowed on the receipts side, received on the payments side) — never trade discount.

options.text: It is debited to Discount Allowed A/c when granted
options.explanation: Discount Allowed A/c records CASH discount on prompt receipts — trade discount never reaches any account.

options.text: It is credited to the customer's account at year end
options.explanation: There is nothing to credit — the sale was recorded net from the start.

options.text: It is never recorded separately — transactions are entered net of it
options.explanation: Correct. Trade discount is a deduction from the list price shown on the invoice; the books see only the net figure.

questions.sourceRef: Trade discount never recorded; entries net of it

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Accounting Process · Cash book discount columns
questions.stem: In March, Anand Traders received ₹19,600 from Bela in full settlement of her account of ₹20,000, and ₹14,550 from Chirag in full settlement of ₹15,000. At month end, the discount-allowed column of the triple-column cash book is:

options.text: Totalled at ₹850, the total being posted to the debit of Discount Allowed A/c
options.explanation: Correct. Bela's discount 400 + Chirag's 450 = ₹850. Discount columns are memoranda columns — totalled, never balanced — and the period total posts in one stroke to Discount Allowed A/c (a loss, so debit).
This picks up only Chirag's discount and misses Bela's ₹400 (20,000 − 19,600).
This picks up only Bela's discount and misses Chirag's ₹450 (15,000 − 14,550).
This counts each discount twice (850 × 2) — as if a leg were entered on both sides. Each discount sits once, in the debit-side discount column only.

questions.sourceRef: Discount columns: totalled not balanced; total → Discount Allowed A/c (Dr)

questions.stem: Anand Traders' cash book for March 2026: opening cash ₹9,000; cash sales ₹26,500; deposited ₹15,000 cash into the bank; paid wages ₹4,800 in cash; withdrew ₹3,000 from the bank for shop use; paid electricity ₹2,200 in cash. The closing balance of the CASH column is:

options.explanation: This ignores the cash leg of the ₹15,000 deposit — a contra entry has a leg in BOTH columns: bank debited AND cash credited.
Correct. 9,000 + 26,500 − 15,000 (contra: cash to bank) − 4,800 + 3,000 (contra: bank to cash) − 2,200 = ₹16,500.
This treats the ₹3,000 withdrawal as a cash PAYMENT instead of a receipt — the money came INTO the till from the bank, so the cash column is debited.
This drops the ₹3,000 withdrawal entirely, as if marking it 'C' meant no entry — the 'C' only means no ledger posting; both cash-book legs are still made.

questions.sourceRef: Cash column with contra entries both ways

questions.stem: Continuing Anand Traders' March 2026 cash book: opening bank balance ₹42,000; cheque of ₹14,700 from Bela banked the same day; ₹15,000 cash deposited into the bank; paid Prakash by cheque ₹9,800; withdrew ₹3,000 from the bank for shop use; bank charges ₹250. The closing balance of the BANK column is:

options.explanation: This misses the bank leg of the ₹3,000 withdrawal — when cash is drawn for office use, the bank column is credited even though the entry is a contra.
This ignores the bank charges of ₹250 — charges are a real payment through the bank column (and NOT a contra; the bank is the other party, not the till).
This misses the bank leg of the ₹15,000 deposit — the deposit debits the bank column; only the ledger posting is dispensed with.

questions.sourceRef: Bank column: cheques in, contras both ways, charges out

questions.stem: Nikhil Traders' bank column opens with an OVERDRAFT of ₹12,000. During the month, cheques of ₹30,000 were deposited and payments of ₹26,500 were made by cheque. The closing bank column shows:

options.explanation: The arithmetic is right but the reading is wrong — a net CREDIT of 8,500 means the firm still owes the bank; that is an overdraft, not money in the bank.
This reverses deposits and payments (−12,000 − 30,000 + 26,500) — deposits reduce an overdraft; payments deepen it.
This treats the opening overdraft as a favourable balance of 12,000 (12,000 + 30,000 − 26,500) — an overdraft opens on the CREDIT side.
Correct. −12,000 + 30,000 − 26,500 = −8,500 — still a credit balance, i.e. an overdraft of ₹8,500. The bank column is the one cash-book column that CAN sit in credit.

questions.sourceRef: Bank column may show credit balance = overdraft

questions.stem: Meena's double-column cash book shows cash ₹5,000 and bank ₹40,000. She withdraws ₹10,000 from the bank for office use and marks both legs 'C'. Immediately after this entry, the cash and bank balances are:

options.explanation: Correct. The contra debits the cash column ₹10,000 (money into the till) and credits the bank column ₹10,000 — both legs inside the cash book, nothing posted to any ledger account.
This records only the cash leg — the money did not appear from nowhere; the bank column must be credited.
This treats 'C' as meaning 'entered elsewhere, skip the cash book' — the 'C' means the OPPOSITE: both legs live inside the cash book, and only the ledger posting is skipped.
This records only the bank leg — the withdrawal reduces the bank AND swells the till; a contra always has two legs.

questions.sourceRef: Contra: debit cash column, credit bank column (or vice versa), no posting

questions.stem: Meena received a cheque of ₹9,750 from Dinesh in full settlement of his account of ₹10,000. The amount entered in the discount-allowed column is:

options.explanation: This doubles the discount, as if it were entered on both sides — the discount sits once, in the debit-side column only.
Correct. 10,000 − 9,750 = ₹250 — a cash discount for prompt settlement, entered in the discount-allowed column on the receipts side; Dinesh's account is credited with the full ₹10,000.

options.text: Nil — settlement discounts are never recorded
options.explanation: This confuses cash discount with TRADE discount. Trade discount is never recorded; CASH discount is — Discount Allowed is a real loss account.
That is the cheque amount, which goes in the BANK (or cash) column — the discount column takes only the ₹250 concession.

questions.sourceRef: Cash discount = amount due − amount accepted in full settlement

questions.stem: The cash book is unusual among the books of account because it is:

options.text: Only a memorandum record with no place in the double entry
options.explanation: Its columns ARE the cash and bank accounts — fully part of the double entry. (Only the discount columns are memoranda.)

options.text: A subsidiary book whose total is posted monthly to the Cash A/c
options.explanation: The goods books work by totals posted to ledger accounts; the cash book IS the ledger account — nothing is posted to any Cash A/c.

options.text: Both a book of original entry and the ledger account for cash and bank
options.explanation: Correct. Cash transactions are recorded here FIRST (original entry), and no separate Cash A/c is opened in the ledger — the cash book plays both roles at once.

options.text: Only a book of original entry — a separate Cash A/c is kept in the ledger
options.explanation: No separate Cash A/c exists when a cash book is kept — that would duplicate every entry.

questions.sourceRef: Cash book = book of original entry + ledger account

questions.stem: Which of the following is a CONTRA entry in a double or triple-column cash book?

options.text: Bank charges debited by the bank
options.explanation: The other leg is Bank Charges A/c (an expense) — the bank is charging for services, not moving money between the till and the account.

options.text: A cheque received from a customer and banked the same day
options.explanation: One leg (bank) is in the cash book, but the other leg is the CUSTOMER's account — a normal entry, not cash-to-bank movement.

options.text: Cash withdrawn from the bank for the proprietor's personal use
options.explanation: That is Drawings — a real posting to Drawings A/c is needed, so it is not a contra even though it looks similar.

options.text: Cash withdrawn from the bank for office use
options.explanation: Correct. Money moved BETWEEN cash and bank — both legs sit inside the cash book, marked 'C', with no ledger posting.

questions.sourceRef: Contra = movement between cash and bank; personal withdrawal = Drawings

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Accounting Process · Cash book discount columns
questions.stem: The discount columns of a triple-column cash book are:

options.text: Totalled, never balanced — the totals are posted to Discount Allowed A/c (Dr) and Discount Received A/c (Cr)
options.explanation: Correct. They are memoranda columns: each period's totals go in one stroke to the two discount accounts in the ledger.

options.text: Posted entry by entry to each customer's and supplier's account only
options.explanation: The personal accounts do get their full-settlement credits/debits, but the COLUMN totals must still reach the two discount accounts — that is the posting the question asks about.

options.text: Balanced like the cash and bank columns, and the balance carried down
options.explanation: The discount columns are not accounts — there is no balance to carry. Only the cash and bank columns are balanced.

options.text: Netted against each other, only the difference being posted
options.explanation: Discount allowed is a loss and discount received a gain — two different accounts; netting them would bury both figures.

questions.sourceRef: Discount columns are memoranda: totalled, not balanced

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Accounting Process · Cash book balances
questions.stem: Which of the following balances is IMPOSSIBLE in a cash book?

options.text: A debit balance in the cash column
options.explanation: The normal state — cash in hand.

options.text: A credit balance in the cash column
options.explanation: Correct — impossible. You cannot pay out more physical cash than the till holds; the cash column can only show a debit balance. Any option showing a credit cash balance is self-condemned.

options.text: A debit balance in the bank column
options.explanation: The normal state — a favourable bank balance.

options.text: A credit balance in the bank column
options.explanation: Perfectly possible — that is an overdraft, where the bank lets you pay out more than you deposited.

questions.sourceRef: Cash column: debit balance only; bank column may be overdrawn

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Accounting Process · Petty cash imprest
questions.stem: Sethi Stores runs petty cash on the imprest system with a float of ₹6,000. During April the petty cashier paid: postage ₹1,240, cartage ₹860, stationery ₹1,375 and staff refreshments ₹525. On 1 May the chief cashier reimburses:

options.explanation: This adds the imprest and the expenses together (6,000 + 4,000) — the chief cashier replaces only what left the box.
This advances the full imprest again — added to the ₹2,000 still in hand, the petty cashier would hold ₹8,000, breaking the fixed-float rule.
Correct. Reimbursement = total petty expenses of the period = 1,240 + 860 + 1,375 + 525 = ₹4,000 — exactly what was spent, restoring the float to the ₹6,000 imprest.
That is the cash still IN HAND (6,000 − 4,000), not the reimbursement — topping up by the in-hand amount would leave the float at ₹4,000.

questions.sourceRef: Imprest: reimbursement = period's petty expenses

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Accounting Process · Petty cash imprest
questions.stem: A petty cash float of ₹5,000 is maintained on the imprest system. Expenses of ₹3,720 were paid during the month. The cash with the petty cashier just BEFORE reimbursement, and just AFTER, is:

options.explanation: Before reimbursement the cashier holds only what expenses left behind — ₹1,280 in cash; the other ₹3,720 exists as vouchers, not cash.
This forgets the reimbursement entirely — the whole point of the imprest system is that the float is restored to ₹5,000 each period.
₹3,720 is what was SPENT, not what remains — in-hand cash is the float minus the spending.
Correct. Before: 5,000 − 3,720 = ₹1,280 in hand (plus vouchers for 3,720 — together always equal to the imprest). After the chief cashier reimburses ₹3,720, the float returns to ₹5,000.

questions.sourceRef: Cash in hand = imprest − expenses; restored to imprest on reimbursement

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Accounting Process · Petty cash imprest
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of the imprest system of petty cash?

options.text: The float grows every period by the amount reimbursed
options.explanation: Correct — this is NOT a feature. The float stays FIXED: reimbursement equals what was spent, so the cashier starts every period with the same imprest amount.

options.text: The chief cashier reviews every voucher before reimbursing
options.explanation: This IS a feature — the reimbursement step doubles as a control check.

options.text: The petty cashier always holds cash plus vouchers equal to the imprest
options.explanation: This IS a feature — it makes the system self-policing at any moment.

options.text: The analytical columns give ready-made totals for posting each expense head
options.explanation: This IS a feature of the analytical petty cash book — one column per expense head (postage, cartage, stationery…).

questions.sourceRef: Imprest = fixed float; self-policing; analytical columns

questions.stem: The ledger balances of Lakshmi Traders on 31 March: capital ₹2,00,000; purchases ₹1,50,000; sales ₹2,40,000; returns inward ₹5,000; returns outward ₹4,000; cash ₹30,000; debtors ₹80,000; creditors ₹50,000; wages ₹39,000; machinery ₹1,90,000. If every balance is placed on its correct side, the trial balance totals:

options.explanation: This adds the two columns together — each column separately totals 4,94,000; the 'total' of a trial balance means one column's figure.

Correct. Debit column: purchases 1,50,000 + returns inward 5,000 + cash 30,000 + debtors 80,000 + wages 39,000 + machinery 1,90,000 = 4,94,000. Credit column: capital 2,00,000 + sales 2,40,000 + returns outward 4,000 + creditors 50,000 = 4,94,000 — the two columns agree.
This puts returns inward in the CREDIT column (4,94,000 − 5,000). Returns inward (sales returns) carries a debit balance — 'returns' does not automatically mean credit.
This puts returns outward in the DEBIT column (4,94,000 + 4,000) — purchase returns carry a credit balance, sitting opposite purchases.

questions.sourceRef: Debit column: assets, expenses, drawings, returns inward; credit: liabilities, capital, incomes, returns outward

questions.stem: An agreed trial balance is conclusive proof of:

options.explanation: A transaction completely omitted disturbs NOTHING — both its debit and its credit are missing equally.

options.text: The accuracy of the profit for the year
options.explanation: An error of principle (say, repairs capitalised) distorts profit while the trial balance agrees happily.

options.text: Arithmetical accuracy only — and even then several classes of error survive it
options.explanation: Correct. The trial balance is a statement (not an account) prepared on a date; agreement proves debits equal credits, nothing more. Complete omission, principle, compensating, wrong-account and original-entry errors all leave it perfectly balanced.

options.text: The correctness of every entry in the books
options.explanation: Five whole families of two-sided error keep the columns equal while the books stay wrong.

questions.sourceRef: Agreed TB = arithmetical accuracy only, never conclusive

questions.stem: Which of the following errors will an agreed trial balance FAIL to disclose?

options.text: The discount-allowed column total never posted to Discount Allowed A/c
options.explanation: Disclosed. The customers' credits are all in place but the answering debit is missing — one aspect unposted is a one-sided error.

options.text: A sale of ₹4,500 posted to the customer's account as ₹5,400
options.explanation: Disclosed. The sales book (and Sales A/c) carry 4,500 but the customer's debit is 5,400 — a wrong amount on ONE side throws the columns out by 900.
Disclosed. An overcast inflates only the debit posting to Purchases A/c — one-sided, so the columns disagree by ₹1,000.

options.text: Repairs to a scooter debited to Vehicles A/c
options.explanation: Correct — not disclosed. An error of principle hits the wrong CLASS of account but keeps a debit against a credit, so both columns stay equal.

questions.sourceRef: TB catches one-sided errors; errors of principle survive

questions.stem: Gopal Traders' trial balance disagreed and the difference was placed in a Suspense Account. Three errors were later found: (i) the purchases book was undercast by ₹3,000; (ii) a credit sale to Ravi of ₹5,400 was posted to his account as ₹4,500; (iii) the discount-allowed column total of ₹800 was never posted to Discount Allowed A/c. The Suspense Account must have been opened with:

options.explanation: Correct. Each error left the DEBIT side short: purchases debit short 3,000 + Ravi's debit short 900 (5,400 − 4,500) + discount debit short 800 = 4,700. The debit column was the shorter one, so Suspense sits there with ₹4,700.
This misses error (iii) — an unposted discount-column total (3,000 + 900) is itself a one-sided error that feeds the difference.
Right figure, wrong side — Suspense goes on the SHORTER column, and here every error starved the debit column, so the suspense balance is a debit.
This treats error (ii) as an EXCESS debit of 900 to be deducted (3,000 + 800 − 900) — Ravi was debited 4,500 instead of 5,400, so his debit is SHORT by 900, adding to the shortfall.

questions.sourceRef: Suspense = net one-sided difference, placed on the shorter column

questions.stem: A credit purchase of ₹6,200 from Karan, correctly entered in the purchases book, was posted to the DEBIT of Karan's account. In the rectification entry (through Suspense), Karan's account is credited with:

options.text: Nil — the error is two-sided and needs no suspense entry
options.explanation: The purchases DEBIT was posted correctly from the book; only Karan's posting went wrong — a one-sided error, which is exactly what Suspense exists to absorb.

Correct. Karan should have a credit of 6,200 but instead carries a debit of 6,200 — so the correction must be 6,200 to cancel the wrong debit PLUS 6,200 to create the missing credit: Suspense A/c Dr 12,400 — To Karan A/c 12,400.
This rectifies only one side — it cancels the wrong debit but never records the credit that should have existed; Karan would still show nil instead of owing-to-him 6,200.
This halves the amount, as if the error were shared between two accounts — the purchases book (and Purchases A/c) were correct; the whole error lives in Karan's account.

questions.sourceRef: Wrong-side posting: rectify with DOUBLE the amount

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Accounting Process · Effect on profit
questions.stem: Kartik Traders reports a draft net profit of ₹1,80,000. Before finalisation, five errors surface: (i) repairs of ₹12,000 were debited to Machinery A/c; (ii) the sales book was overcast by ₹5,000; (iii) the purchases book was overcast by ₹7,000; (iv) a credit sale of ₹15,000 was completely omitted; (v) stationery of ₹2,500 was debited to Purchases A/c. The corrected net profit is:

options.explanation: This flips error (i), ADDING 12,000 instead of deducting — capitalised REPAIRS mean an expense is missing from the P&L, so rectification reduces profit (unlike capitalisable wages wrongly expensed, which raise it).
This ignores the omitted credit sale of 15,000 — a completely omitted transaction still changes profit once recorded, even though it never disturbed the trial balance.

Correct. 1,80,000 − 12,000 (repairs expense was omitted from P&L, hidden in Machinery) − 5,000 (sales income overstated) + 7,000 (purchases expense overstated) + 15,000 (sale income omitted) + 0 (stationery-in-purchases moves gross profit only) = ₹1,85,000.
This also deducts the stationery of 2,500 — but a swap between two expense heads charged against profit leaves NET profit unchanged; only the gross profit moves.

questions.sourceRef: Corrected profit = draft + overstated expenses + omitted incomes − omitted expenses − overstated incomes

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Accounting Process · Effect on profit
questions.stem: Sharma Fabricators' draft profit is ₹96,000. It is then found that wages of ₹20,000 paid for installing a new lathe were debited to Wages A/c. The corrected profit is:

options.explanation: This adds the 20,000 twice (96,000 + 40,000) — one rectification entry, one effect.
This treats it as a zero-effect swap between expense heads — but this swap crosses the capital/revenue line (an error of principle), so profit genuinely changes.
Direction flipped — this deducts 20,000, treating the error as an omitted expense; the expense was OVERSTATED, so rectifying adds it back.

Correct. Installation wages are capital expenditure (part of the lathe's cost) — the P&L carried an expense it should not have, so profit was UNDERSTATED: 96,000 + 20,000 = ₹1,16,000. Rectification: Machinery A/c Dr 20,000 — To Wages A/c 20,000.

questions.sourceRef: Capital expenditure in a revenue head understates profit by that amount

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Accounting Process · Effect on profit
questions.stem: Verma Stores' draft NET profit is ₹1,25,000. It is discovered that stationery of ₹3,000 was debited to Purchases A/c. After rectification, the net profit is:

options.explanation: Correct. Removing 3,000 from Purchases raises gross profit by 3,000, but charging the same 3,000 as Stationery takes it straight back — the examiner's favourite zero-effect trap. Only the GROSS profit moves.
This rectifies the purchases side but forgets that the stationery expense must now be charged — the 3,000 does not vanish; it changes address.
This adds the 3,000 twice (once out of purchases, once as an imagined income) — no income is involved anywhere in this error.
This charges the stationery again WITHOUT removing it from purchases — double-counting the same 3,000 of expense.

questions.sourceRef: Swap between expense heads: gross profit moves, net profit unchanged

questions.stem: Mahesh Traders opened a Suspense Account with a debit balance of ₹600. Two errors were then found: (i) the purchases book was overcast by ₹3,400; (ii) a credit sale to Meera of ₹4,000, correctly entered in the sales book, was never posted to her account. After both rectifications, the Suspense Account shows:

options.explanation: This rectifies only (i) (600 + 3,400) and leaves Meera's missing posting uncorrected — the account cannot close until every one-sided error is fixed.

Correct. (i) is one-sided (excess purchases debit): Suspense A/c Dr 3,400 — To Purchases A/c. (ii) is one-sided (Meera's debit missing): Meera A/c Dr 4,000 — To Suspense A/c. Suspense: Dr 600 + 3,400 = 4,000 against Cr 4,000 — closes to nil, proving the hunt is over.
This treats the overcast (i) as two-sided and routes only (ii) through Suspense (600 Dr − 4,000 Cr) — an overcast book is the textbook ONE-sided error; its correction must pass through Suspense.
This routes NEITHER error through Suspense, treating both as two-sided — but each disturbed only one side of the books, which is exactly why the trial balance disagreed in the first place.

questions.sourceRef: Suspense closes to nil when all one-sided errors are rectified

questions.stem: Repairs to a delivery van debited to Vehicles A/c is an example of an error of:

options.explanation: No second error cancels this one — it stands alone, silently overstating profit.
Commission errors stay within the same class — wrong amount, wrong account of the SAME kind, wrong side, or wrong casting. Here the error crosses from revenue to capital.
Correct. Right amount, wrong CLASS of account — revenue expenditure (repairs) treated as capital (an asset). The trial balance still agrees, but expenses are understated and assets overstated.
Nothing was left half-recorded — both a debit and a credit exist; they simply sit in the wrong class of account.

questions.sourceRef: Error of principle = capital/revenue confusion; TB unaffected

questions.stem: Compensating errors are:

options.text: Errors of principle committed in two accounts at once
options.explanation: Compensating errors can be of any kind — what defines them is the mutual cancellation, not the class of account involved.

options.text: One-sided errors that the Suspense Account compensates for
options.explanation: Suspense parks the net difference of one-sided errors; compensating errors, by definition, produce NO difference for suspense to hold.

options.text: Errors corrected by paying compensation to the affected party
options.explanation: No party is compensated — 'compensating' describes the errors offsetting EACH OTHER arithmetically.

options.text: Two or more errors whose effects cancel each other, leaving the trial balance agreed
options.explanation: Correct. An excess debit of ₹500 in one account offset by an excess credit of ₹500 elsewhere — each error is real, but their net effect on the columns is nil.

questions.sourceRef: Compensating errors: mutual cancellation, TB agreed

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Accounting Process · Rectification after final accounts
questions.stem: An error affecting a nominal account is discovered in the NEXT year, after the final accounts have been prepared and closed. The rectification entry uses:

options.text: The Profit & Loss Adjustment A/c in place of the nominal account, its final balance going to Capital A/c
options.explanation: Correct. Last year's nominal accounts are already closed into last year's profit and cannot be reopened — P&L Adjustment stands in for them, and its balance transfers to Capital.

options.text: The Suspense Account in every case
options.explanation: Suspense handles the missing leg of ONE-sided errors; the P&L Adjustment route answers a different problem — closed nominal accounts. (A one-sided error found now may touch both.)

options.text: The same nominal account, reopened for the correction
options.explanation: The nominal account was closed to Trading/P&L at year end — debiting or crediting it now would distort THIS year's expenses with LAST year's error.
Feeding last year's error into this year's Trading Account misstates this year's gross profit — the whole point of P&L Adjustment is to keep it out.

questions.sourceRef: Stage 3 rectification: P&L Adjustment A/c → Capital A/c

questions.stem: State the three golden rules of debit and credit under the traditional classification, and classify each of the following accounts: (a) Outstanding Rent A/c, (b) Goodwill A/c, (c) Drawings A/c, (d) Nashik Urban Co-operative Bank A/c. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Personal accounts: debit the receiver, credit the giver
Real accounts: debit what comes in, credit what goes out
Nominal accounts: debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains
(a) Outstanding Rent — representative personal (stands for the landlord owed); (b) Goodwill — intangible real
(c) Drawings — personal (the owner's account, not nominal); (d) the bank — artificial personal, not real

questions.sourceRef: Golden rules + classification traps

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Accounting Process · Trade vs cash discount
questions.stem: Distinguish between trade discount and cash discount (any four points of difference), and state how each is treated in the books of account. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Purpose: trade discount — deduction from LIST price for bulk orders/dealers; cash discount — reward for PROMPT payment
Recording: trade discount never appears in any account (entries made net); cash discount IS recorded — Discount Allowed A/c (loss) or Discount Received A/c (gain)
Where shown: trade discount on the invoice only; cash discount in the discount columns of the triple-column cash book (allowed on debit side, received on credit side)
Timing/base: trade discount at the time of sale, on the list price; cash discount at the time of settlement, on the amount due

questions.sourceRef: Trade vs cash discount distinctions

questions.stem: Prepare the triple-column cash book of Nirmal Traders for June 2026: Jun 1 — cash in hand ₹8,000, bank balance ₹25,000. Jun 4 — received a cheque of ₹19,600 from Nisha in full settlement of her account of ₹20,000, banked the same day. Jun 8 — cash sales ₹14,500. Jun 12 — deposited ₹10,000 cash into the bank. Jun 18 — paid Prakash by cheque ₹7,840 in full settlement of ₹8,000. Jun 22 — withdrew ₹2,500 from the bank for office use. Jun 27 — paid shop rent ₹3,000 in cash. Balance the cash and bank columns and total the discount columns. (8 marks)

skeleton.point: Jun 4: bank column Dr 19,600; discount-allowed column 400 (20,000 − 19,600); Nisha's account credited with the full 20,000
skeleton.citation: full settlement → cash discount in discount column

skeleton.point: Jun 12 and Jun 22 are contra entries marked 'C': Jun 12 cash Cr 10,000 / bank Dr 10,000; Jun 22 bank Cr 2,500 / cash Dr 2,500 — neither posted to any ledger account
skeleton.citation: contra entries within the cash book

skeleton.point: Discount columns TOTALLED, not balanced: allowed 400 → Discount Allowed A/c (Dr); received 160 (8,000 − 7,840) → Discount Received A/c (Cr)

questions.sourceRef: Triple-column cash book with contras and both discounts

questions.stem: What is a trial balance? State its purposes, the methods of preparing it, and the errors an agreed trial balance fails to disclose. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: A STATEMENT (not an account, not part of the double entry) listing every ledger balance — debits in one column, credits in the other — on a particular date
Purposes: checks arithmetical accuracy; supplies the raw material for final accounts; gives a bird's-eye view of all accounts
Methods: balance method (standard — closing balances), total method (gross totals of each side), compound method (both sets of columns)
Errors NOT disclosed: complete omission; errors of principle; compensating errors; posting to the wrong account on the right side with the right amount; wrong amount in the book of original entry
skeleton.citation: two-sided errors survive an agreed TB

questions.sourceRef: TB nature, purposes, methods, limits

questions.stem: Explain the classes of errors in accounting with one example of each, and state which of them disturb the agreement of the trial balance. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Error of principle: right amount, wrong CLASS of account (capital/revenue confused) — e.g. repairs debited to Machinery A/c; TB not disturbed
Error of omission: complete (credit sale never recorded anywhere — TB not disturbed) vs partial (entered in sales book, never posted to the customer — TB disturbed)
Error of commission: wrong amount, wrong account of the SAME class, wrong side, or wrong casting — e.g. sale to Mohan posted to Sohan; purchases book overcast
Compensating errors: two or more errors cancelling each other — e.g. excess debit of ₹500 offset by an excess credit of ₹500; TB not disturbed
Working rule: ONE-SIDED errors (overcast/undercast, wrong-side or wrong-amount posting on one side, one aspect unposted) disturb the TB; TWO-SIDED errors keep it agreed

questions.sourceRef: Error classification and TB effect

questions.stem: The trial balance of Hari Om Stores was short on the DEBIT side by ₹2,700 and the difference was placed in a Suspense Account. Later, three errors were found: (i) the sales book was overcast by ₹3,500; (ii) a credit purchase from Hari of ₹4,200 was posted to his account as ₹3,400; (iii) repairs of ₹900 to the shop building were debited to Building A/c. Pass rectification entries and prepare the Suspense Account. (8 marks)

skeleton.point: (i) Sales A/c Dr 3,500 — To Suspense A/c 3,500 (the sales book total posts to the CREDIT of Sales; an overcast is 3,500 of excess credit — one-sided, so Suspense takes the other leg)
skeleton.citation: overcast sales book = one-sided excess credit

skeleton.point: (ii) Suspense A/c Dr 800 — To Hari A/c 800 (Hari credited 3,400 instead of 4,200 — a short credit of 800, one-sided)
(iii) Repairs A/c Dr 900 — To Building A/c 900 (error of principle, two-sided — Suspense is NOT touched)
Suspense Account: debit side — opening balance b/d 2,700 + Hari 800 = 3,500; credit side — Sales 3,500; the account closes to nil, proving all one-sided errors are found
Consistency check: (i) put 3,500 excess in the credit column, (ii) left it 800 short — net credit excess 2,700, matching the debit-side shortfall of 2,700

questions.sourceRef: Suspense rectification with mixed one- and two-sided errors
